extracted.intended_audience: students, artists, writers, composers, and theorists interested in aesthetics (theory of the sublime and the beautiful)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria from a philosophical account of beauty and the sublime to evaluate or produce aesthetic works across senses (visual art, music, tactile design, literary description). Focuses on properties that produce pleasure (beauty) versus those that produce awe/astonishment (sublime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of sudden variation / smooth gradual change
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface may continually vary its direction, but it never varies it suddenly; the quick application of anything sudden is disagreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudden changes (even slight ones like an unexpected warm or cold touch, or an unexpected tap) startle and produce displeasure. In visual form and tactile design favor gradual, insensible deviations rather than abrupt angles or shocks. Example anti-pattern: angular figures, sudden shifts in outline that produce a 'climbing or falling in miniature'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness and unangular forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft, smooth, variated, unangular bodies are pleasurable to touch and sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounded, soft shapes and surfaces afford pleasure; squares, triangles, and other angular figures are generally not beautiful to sight or feeling. When designing for beauty, prioritize soft textures and rounded contours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑sensory analogy and concordance of pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of different senses (sight, touch, hearing, taste, smell) agree and can illuminate one another; similar dispositions (softness, winding, unbroken continuance) recur across senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies between senses (e.g., describe sights in tactile or musical terms) to clarify aesthetic aims. Where multiple senses concur in a quality, we may more confidently name it beautiful. Example: colors and dispositions found beautiful to sight would likely be agreeable to touch if touch could discern them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful sounds: soft, clear, even, smooth, weak
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful in music agrees best with sounds that are clear, even, smooth, and weak; it will not bear loudness, strength, shrillness, harshness, or excessive depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke beauty in sound or musical writing, prefer delicate timbres, gentle dynamics, and clear, even tones. Avoid shrill or harsh notes and abrupt loudness intended to raise tumultuous passions. Example: Milton's 'soft Lydian airs' are cited as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rapid variety and quick transitions in music
rubrics_metrics.description: Great variety and quick transitions from one measure or tone to another are contrary to the genius of the beautiful in music; such transitions excite mirth or tumult rather than the languor characterizing beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For beauty aim for slow, gradual development and restrained variation. Rapid modulations or frequent metric/tonal changes produce lively or comic effects, not the 'melting' or 'languor' associated with beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional character: beauty induces languor/melancholy, not mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: The passion excited by beauty is nearer to a species of melancholy than to jollity and mirth; beauty's effect is sinking, melting, languor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or judging beautiful works, look for a gentle, soft-moving emotional tone rather than buoyant cheerfulness. The intended affect is subdued, tender, and consolatory rather than exuberant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrastive property pairs: sublime versus beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublime objects are vast, rugged, dark, solid, and massive; beautiful objects are comparatively small, smooth, polished, light, and delicate. Beauty shuns strict right lines (deviating insensibly), whereas the great (sublime) in many cases loves the right line or makes strong deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use opposing qualities deliberately depending on aim: to produce beauty choose small-scale, polished, delicate, subtly curved forms and clarity; to produce the sublime choose vastness, ruggedness, darkness/gloom, solidity, and occasionally imposing right lines or strong deviations. When many properties align toward the same effect the passion produced is more uniform and powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of association vs natural properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Some effects on the passions arise from associations formed early in life; however, one should first seek natural properties of things as causes of our passions before attributing effects solely to association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In aesthetic analysis distinguish between (a) natural, immediate effects of qualities (e.g., darkness causing uncertainty) and (b) culturally or individually acquired associations (e.g., ghosts associated with night). Evaluate whether a reaction is likely innate/natural or associative when explaining audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime derives from a mode of terror/pain (tension without real harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime is built on terror or a passion like it: whatever produces an unnatural tension of the nerves (as terror does) can be a source of the sublime, even if no real danger is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the sublime, create impressions that bring the perceiver close to a state resembling fear or pain (tension, expectation, astonishment) without actual harm—producing a 'delightful horror' or 'tranquillity tinged with terror.' Degrees: astonishment (highest), then awe, reverence, respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of pain/terror: non‑noxious stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain or terror must be so modified as not to be actually noxious; if pain is carried to violence or terror pertains to present destruction, it ceases to produce the sublime's delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the threat implied or aestheticized—intensity should approach but not cross into genuine danger or harm. Employ suggestive tension, scale, or apprehension rather than immediate, harmful stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of dimension (vastness) produces the sublime via bodily strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual objects great in their dimensions produce sublimity because they strain the sensory organs (e.g., the eye traversing extensive space), producing tension approaching pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual composition or description, introduce impressive scale or magnitude that resists easy comprehension and compels the perceiver's attention to traverse or linger, thereby increasing sensory tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform succession and repetition (the artificial infinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform succession of great, similar parts (e.g., a colonnade of identical pillars in a right line) produces the sublime via repeated similar impressions that 'work up' the sensory organs to near pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition of similar elements along a perceivable axis to build cumulative tension. Avoid alternating dissimilar elements (round then square) which interrupt and relax the sensory impression. The succession should be simple, uniform in disposition, shape, and coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and consistency of vibrations/impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibrations (impressions) must be similar at every impression; dissimilar successive impulses prevent accumulation of effect needed for the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure repeat elements are sufficiently alike so that each reinforces the previous impression rather than replacing it. In sound, repeated similar strokes (with expectation and surprise) augment tension; in sight, repeated identical motifs do the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition must detain the attention, not merely be vast
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare wall, though vast, is less sublime than a colonnade because it gives one single idea and does not detain the eye with a succession of similar impulses; succession that detains is key to sublimity, not mere vastness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences so that the viewer’s attention is compelled to proceed along them and be held—e.g., rhythm, spacing, or interruptions that sustain expectation—rather than presenting a single monotonous surface that is quickly encompassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expectation and surprise in temporal arts (sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hearing, repeated strokes produce expectation; expectation itself causes tension, and the surprise at return of the stroke further increases tension, helping reach the verge of pain and thus the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In music or narrative sound design employ recurring motifs with irregular return-timing or sustained anticipation to build tension. Expectation + surprise amplifies the sublime effect—example: successive firing of cannon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkness/blackness and obscurity as sources of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness and blackness can be naturally terrible and thus sources of the sublime because utter darkness creates ignorance of safety and imminent danger; this may be innate beyond mere cultural association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obscurity, shadow, or blackness to induce uncertainty and latent fear. In literature and visual design, strategic opacity and concealment can evoke terror-like tension that contributes to the sublime. Historical anecdote: a newly sighted boy reacted with uneasiness to black objects, suggesting a natural effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize bodily correlates (tension/strain) when designing for emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions correspond to bodily affections (tension, contraction); aesthetic causes operate by producing bodily dispositions that in turn produce mental emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a specific affective response, consider how form, scale, repetition, and sensory patterns will physically 'brace' the perceiver (eye movement, auditory expectation, tactile anticipation) to elicit the intended emotion.
